text: # Gliomas — Clinical Overview
heading: Overview
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Epidemiology

There are approximately 6 cases of gliomas diagnosed per 100,000 individuals
every year in the United States. Among the roughly 80,000-90,000 newly
diagnosed primary brain tumors annually, roughly 25% are gliomas.
Glioblastomas specifically account for about 12,000 cases yearly,
representing approximately 15% of all newly diagnosed brain tumors and 50%
of malignant cases.
heading: Epidemiology
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Clinical Presentation

Common symptoms include headaches, seizures, nausea, vomiting, and focal
neurological deficits. Physical examination findings may reveal focal
weakness, sensory loss, or altered consciousness from mass effect and edema.
Approximately 3-10% of low-grade lesions are discovered incidentally during
unrelated investigations.
heading: Clinical Presentation
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Imaging Characteristics

MRI serves as the primary diagnostic tool for gliomas. Low-grade tumors
typically lack enhancement, while high-grade variants demonstrate variable
enhancement patterns. Gliomas commonly show strong peripheral enhancement
around a necrotic core with a pronounced mass effect, evidenced by
significant midline shift in more aggressive cases. MRI effectively
evaluates cerebral edema and tumor characteristics. Additional imaging
includes head CT for acute findings, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT for metastatic
workup, spinal MRI for ependymomas, and diffusion tensor imaging for
surgical planning near eloquent cortex.
heading: Imaging Characteristics
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Grading and Classification

The 2021 WHO classification incorporates molecular markers (IDH mutations
and 1p/19q co-deletions) alongside histopathology. Astrocytomas are
classified by IDH status; oligodendrogliomas require both IDH mutation and
1p/19q co-deletion; glioblastomas are IDH-wildtype only.
heading: Grading and Classification
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Management

Standard treatment involves maximal safe resection combined with
chemoradiation. The Stupp protocol represents standard care for high-grade
tumors: 60 Gy radiotherapy over 6 weeks with concurrent temozolomide.
Low-grade lesions may require only surgical resection with monitoring.
heading: Management
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text: # Meningioma — Clinical Overview
heading: Overview
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Epidemiology

Meningiomas represent approximately 37.6% of central nervous system tumors,
with an incidence of 9.73 per 100,000 people annually in the United States
(2016-2020). The mean presentation age is 66 years, with a female-to-male
ratio of 2.3:1. The majority of meningiomas are benign and classified as WHO
grade 1 tumors. Among older adults (75-84 years), incidence reaches 37.75
per 100,000, contrasting sharply with 0.14 per 100,000 in children aged
0-19 years.
heading: Epidemiology
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Clinical Presentation

Manifestations vary by location. Parasagittal tumors may cause contralateral
limb paresis, while sphenoid ridge lesions can produce cranial nerve
palsies. Olfactory groove meningiomas can lead to Foster-Kennedy syndrome,
which causes anosmia, contralateral papilledema, and ipsilateral optic
nerve atrophy. Spinal meningiomas typically present with pain and
radiculopathy. Many patients remain asymptomatic, with tumors discovered
incidentally.
heading: Clinical Presentation
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Imaging Characteristics

Brain MRI is the diagnostic standard. On unenhanced sequences, meningiomas
typically appear hypointense on T1-weighted and hyperintense on
T2-weighted imaging. Post-contrast imaging reveals homogeneous enhancement
with the characteristic dural tail sign, distinguishing extra-axial from
intra-axial lesions. The cerebrospinal fluid vascular cleft — CSF trapped
between tumor and cortex — further supports diagnosis. Head CT excels at
detecting calcifications and hyperostosis.
heading: Imaging Characteristics
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## WHO Classification

Distribution follows: 80.1% grade 1 (benign), 18.3% grade 2 (atypical), and
1.5% grade 3 (malignant). Grade 1 tumors include nine histological variants
with benign features. Grade 2 tumors demonstrate increased cellularity,
prominent nuclei, or 4-19 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. Grade 3 lesions
show anaplasia, high mitotic activity (≥20 mitoses/10 high-power fields),
and aggressive behavior.
heading: WHO Classification
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Management

Asymptomatic, small, and slow-growing meningiomas are usually treated with
observation and routine imaging. Symptomatic or enlarging tumors warrant
surgical resection, with the Simpson grading system predicting recurrence
based on resection extent. Gross total resection provides >90% three-year
progression-free survival for benign tumors. Adjuvant radiotherapy improves
outcomes in grade 2-3 disease, while stereotactic radiosurgery offers a
non-surgical alternative.
heading: Management
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text: # Understanding a Normal Brain MRI Report
heading: Overview
source: RadiologyInfo.org (jointly produced by the Radiological Society of North America and the American College of Radiology)

text:
## Overall Purpose

A radiologist interprets brain MRI images and writes a report for the
referring healthcare provider. The report may contain medical terminology,
but patients have the right to access and understand their results.
Questions about a report should be discussed directly with a physician.
heading: Overall Purpose
source: RadiologyInfo.org (jointly produced by the Radiological Society of North America and the American College of Radiology)

text:
## Key Report Sections

**Findings section** — describes what the radiologist observed during the
scan, including the significant absence of concerning features. A
radiologist may use terms like "normal," "unremarkable," or "normal for
patient age." Many things radiologists see on imaging are quite common and
cause no harm.

**Impression section** — the most critical part of the report; it
summarizes the conclusions and recommendations the radiologist wants the
referring provider to be aware of.
heading: Key Report Sections
source: RadiologyInfo.org (jointly produced by the Radiological Society of North America and the American College of Radiology)

text:
## What a Normal/Clear Result Looks Like

When a brain MRI is normal, the report may state findings such as "there is
no evidence of an intracranial mass, bleed, or infarct" or "there is no
abnormal parenchymal or meningeal enhancement." Related phrasing includes
"normal brain MRI," "no acute intracranial abnormality," or "unremarkable
brain MRI."

"No acute intracranial abnormality" specifically means there is no evidence
of an urgent problem inside the skull — no recent stroke, hemorrhage, mass
effect, or other acute finding. It does not rule out chronic changes,
incidental findings, or gradually progressive disease; clinicians integrate
this statement with clinical exam findings, risk factors, and known
age-related MRI changes.
heading: What a Normal/Clear Result Looks Like
source: RadiologyInfo.org (jointly produced by the Radiological Society of North America and the American College of Radiology)

text:
## Common Normal or Incidental Findings

Findings that shouldn't cause alarm on their own include mild brain volume
loss (atrophy), age-related white matter changes, sinus mucosal thickening,
and small cysts — many of these are normal, age-appropriate variations
rather than pathology. A "clear" scan report should still be reviewed with
a physician who can integrate it with the full clinical picture, rather
than interpreted in isolation.
heading: Common Normal or Incidental Findings
source: RadiologyInfo.org (jointly produced by the Radiological Society of North America and the American College of Radiology)

text: # Pituitary Adenoma — Clinical Overview
heading: Overview
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Epidemiology

Pituitary adenomas are remarkably common, with prevalence varying by
detection method. A meta-analysis revealed an average frequency of
pituitary adenomas of 16.7% across studies, though autopsy findings showed
14.4% versus 22.5% on radiological imaging. Clinically relevant adenomas
(those causing symptoms or hormonal effects) occur at significantly lower
rates — approximately 89.1 per 100,000 persons.

The most frequent subtypes include prolactinomas (50% of cases),
nonfunctioning adenomas (30%), somatotroph adenomas (11%), and corticotroph
adenomas (5%). Sex distribution varies by type; prolactinomas
predominantly affect women of reproductive age, while acromegaly is more
common in men.
heading: Epidemiology
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Functioning vs. Nonfunctioning Presentation

Functioning adenomas produce excess hormones causing characteristic
syndromes: prolactinomas cause infertility, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and
erectile dysfunction; growth hormone-secreting adenomas (acromegaly) cause
coarse features, prognathism, arthritis, and carpal tunnel syndrome;
ACTH-secreting adenomas (Cushing disease) cause weight gain, muscle
weakness, moon facies, and purple striae; TSH-secreting adenomas cause
palpitations, weight loss, tremor, and goiter.

Nonfunctioning adenomas cause symptoms through mass effect rather than
hormone secretion, producing visual deficits and hormonal deficiencies from
compression.
heading: Functioning vs. Nonfunctioning Presentation
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Imaging Characteristics

MRI represents the gold standard for evaluation. Adenomas are classified by
size: microadenomas (<10 mm), often incidental findings, usually
asymptomatic; macroadenomas (≥10 mm), more likely to cause compressive
symptoms; giant adenomas (>40 mm). Gadolinium-enhanced coronal and sagittal
T1-weighted images differentiate adenomas from other sellar lesions. Visual
complications occur in approximately 40% to 60% of patients with
suprasellar extension compressing the optic chiasm, typically causing
bitemporal hemianopia.
heading: Imaging Characteristics
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)

text:
## Management

Treatment depends on tumor type and functional status. Nonfunctional
macroadenomas with visual deficits, optic chiasm compression, or
progressive growth warrant transsphenoidal resection. Radiotherapy
addresses residual or recurrent disease.

Prolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists (cabergoline efficacy
>90%), with surgery reserved for medical resistance or pregnancy planning.

GH-secreting adenomas require transsphenoidal surgery as first-line
treatment, achieving IGF-1 normalization in 80-90% of microadenomas and
40-60% of macroadenomas. Somatostatin analogs manage persistent elevation.

ACTH-secreting adenomas demand urgent surgical intervention, achieving
remission (cortisol <2 μg/dL) in 70-90% of cases, with medical therapy
supporting persistent or recurrent disease.
heading: Management
source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine / NIH)
